name: Audio and Video Evidence
title: Audio and Video Evidence
answer: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers recorded calls, voicemail, body camera footage, surveillance video, meeting recordings, and multimedia attachments in email or chat. The work includes locating, preserving, authenticating, transcribing, and reviewing this content for relevance, privilege, and production. Because these files are often large and unstructured, they sit at the intersection of digital forensics, information governance, and litigation support. Practitioners treat the audio or video stream as evidence, not just as a container for metadata.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Audio and video evidence in e-discovery covers recorded calls, voicemail, body camera footage, surveillance video, meeting recordings, and multimedia attachments in email or chat. The work includes locating, preserving, authenticating, transcribing, and reviewing this content for relevance, privilege, and production. Because these files are often large and unstructured, they sit at the intersection of digital forensics, information governance, and litigation support. Practitioners treat the audio or video stream as evidence, not just as a container for metadata.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Processing typically begins with ingestion into an e-discovery platform that can extract audio tracks, generate frame stills, and index spoken words. Storage and compute are often cloud based, with GPU acceleration for transcription and computer vision tasks. The site's directory of 732 AI tools includes utilities for speech to text, speaker separation, and object or face detection, though many law firms use a small set of vetted platforms. Bandwidth and chain of custody matter because original files must remain unaltered while derivative transcripts and clips are created.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Reviewers use automatic speech recognition to create searchable transcripts, then run keyword searches, privilege screens, and issue coding against the text. Speaker diarization labels who said what, while computer vision can flag scenes, text on screen, or weapons and other objects in video. Human reviewers still verify transcripts, watch or listen to key segments, and resolve gaps where audio is poor or multiple people talk over each other. The output is usually a load file linking the native media, transcript, and coded decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Authentication is a central concern because deepfakes, edited clips, and AI generated voices can enter the record. Counsel must establish chain of custody, hash values, and source metadata for any audio or video file before relying on it. Privacy and privilege issues arise when recordings capture nonparties, children, medical conversations, or attorney client discussion. The site tracks 142 active AI lawsuits, and authentication of AI generated media is a recurring issue in that docket.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Audio and video evidence will become more common as collaboration tools, body cameras, and smart devices generate continuous recordings. Models are improving at low resource transcription, accent handling, and cross modal retrieval that lets a reviewer search a spoken phrase and jump to the exact frame. Courts and rulemakers are beginning to address authentication standards for synthetic media, and e-discovery platforms are adding explainability features so a reviewer can see why a model flagged a segment. The practical trend is toward treating audio and video as first class searchable evidence rather than an afterthought to email and documents.
